newsitem.title: GERMANY: KOHL - GERMANS SHOULD ACCEPT LITTLE, NO WAGE GAINS.
newsitem.headline: KOHL - GERMANS SHOULD ACCEPT LITTLE, NO WAGE GAINS.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said in a newspaper interview on Wednesday that Germans should accept little or no real wage increases for the next few years in a bid to fight the country's record unemployment.

Kohl also told the Bild newspaper the European currency, set to start in 1999, would give Europe "strong impulses" for growth and that austerity measures to meet criteria to join the euro did not contradict Bonn's fight against unemployment.

"I find it absolutely reasonable that everyone who has a job should for a few years curb their demands or even completely do without a real increase in wages so that the employment chances for those who are unemployed will improve," Kohl said.
"For most people it would not involve real cuts but merely doing without growth in prosperity," he said in the Bild interview.
Kohl said it was an issue affecting other European nations, particularly France.

In addition, Kohl said in the interview that there was "absolutely no contradiction" between Bonn's efforts to whip Germany's finances into shape for currency union and fighting the country's unemployment, now at a post-war record.
"Currency union with the Euro will give the European economy a strong impulse," Kohl said. "That will also help to create new jobs."

Kohl said Bonn's budget-cutting measures were absolutely necessary to break "the vicious circle" of Germany's growing debt problems and rising interest burden and that "nothing would be won" for the unemployed by increasing debt levels to spur growth.
